content.introduction: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets U.S. monetary policy and oversees open market operations. It consists of the Board of Governors and Reserve Bank presidents. The FOMC influences the federal funds rate and economic policy.
body: The FOMC makes all decisions regarding the conduct of open market operations, which affect the federal funds rate (the rate at which depository institutions lend to each other), the size and composition of the Federal Reserve's asset holdings, and communications with the public about the likely future course of monetary policy. In 1923, they formed the Open Market Investment Committee for these coordinated efforts, which was then transformed into the Open Market Policy Conference in 1930.1 A body called the Federal Open Market Committee was first convened in 1933, following the Glass-Steagall Act; but the FOMC as we know it came into effect only in March of 1936 "as constituted by Section 12A of the Federal Reserve Act as amended by the Banking Act of 1935," as the newly named chairman, Marriner Eccles, explained at that meeting. All members of the Board of Governors and the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York have a permanent voting seat2 on the FOMC; the other 11 Reserve Bank presidents serve on a rotating schedule of one-year terms.

# Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The FOMC is a 12-person committee responsible for setting U.S. monetary policy and overseeing open market operations. Content related to the work of the FOMC can be found on this page, including topics such as the federal funds rate, the FOMC’s Summary of Economic Projections, monetary policy decisions and communications, and the policy framework. ## Explore Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
